tochigi-underground-quarry.intro: A hand-carved quarry the size of a stadium, now an underground cathedral lit for concerts and film shoots.
tochigi-underground-quarry.html:
Descend a narrow staircase into what feels like a cave, opening up into an illuminous void, stretching across 20,000 square meters of carved stone, like the ruins of an underground cathedral. Every piece of stone here was taken out block by block, mostly by hand using pick axes. Each block taking around 4,000 swings to remove.

Workers called kodashi carried out each stone on their backs, strapped to a wooden frame, one block at a time. And each block weighed about 150 kilograms (330 pounds). Machines took over around 1960, and both eras are still legible on the walls, with gouges from the pickaxes alongside the vertical lines left by machine cutting. 

This was a working quarry from 1919 to 1986, extracting Oya stone, which is relatively soft, easy to cut, and became an important building material in the region. Frank Lloyd Wright used large quantities of it in the Imperial Hotel in Tokyo, which opened on the day of the Great Kanto Earthquake in 1923. The hotel was demolished in 1968, but its stone entrance hall and lobby were taken apart block by block and rebuilt at an open-air museum in Aichi.

The quarry was also an important safe house during World War II. During the war, its chambers were used as a secret military airplane manufacturing space, where Nakajima Aircraft ran an underground factory in part of the complex, building fighter planes. After the war, the government used it to store rice.

Now it’s a museum and event space, hosting concerts, exhibitions, theater performances, and film crews. One section, normally closed to visitors, gets built out as a chapel whenever somebody books a wedding. 

Admission is ¥1,000 (about US$6), and the cafe above ground sells coffee and gelato. The temperature underground averages around 8°C (46°F) all year, so dress for the temperature change even in summer!
tochigi-underground-quarry.notes: This place was seriously awesome. The pictures do not do justice to how big this cave feels once your inside. The multicolored illuminated lighting projected on the walls, combined with surreal sculptures littered throughout the cavern really makes it feel like a unique liminal space.

the-place-in-malta-where-people-have-bee.intro: A chequerboard of 350-year-old salt pans cut into the Gozo coast, still harvested by hand each summer.
the-place-in-malta-where-people-have-bee.html:
As Malta is an island nation in the middle of the Mediterranean Sea, it is a natural place for people to make salt from seawater, and in fact, people have been manufacturing salt in Malta since the Phoenicians arrived in the islands.  The most notable place in Malta where people are still making salt using traditional methods is along the north coast of the island of Gozo stretching from Reqqa Point (the northernmost point of the nation of Malta) to Xwejni Bay.  Some places along this coastline feature checkerboards of shallow rectangular pools stretching from the road to the ocean, while others have curved and irregular shallow depressions carved into the limestone rock.

The traditional salt-making process consists of a few steps.  First, water is transferred into larger feeding pools, where evaporation makes the salt more concentrated.  Next, this salt is transferred to shallower pools where the remaining water evaporates, leaving the salt. This usually takes about a week.  Brooms and brushes are then used to sweep up the salt, the salt is gathered into piles, and then the salt is allowed to dry another day before it is transferred into bags and stored away.  Note that salt harvesting takes place between mid-May and the beginning of September when the high temperatures help to evaporate the seawater.  This would be the best time to see people at work among the salt pans.

People have been manufacturing salt here for over 350 years, and at least several generations of one individual family have worked in this location since the mid-nineteenth century.  The harvesters sell their salt from a couple of shops carved into the nearby hillside, although the salt can also be purchased from souvenir shops across the islands.  Additionally, the salt pans themselves are widely considered to be scenic in their own right and have now become a spectacular yet underappreciated tourist attraction on the north shore of Gozo.

These salt pans can be visited at all times of day.  People driving to the site can park across the street from the salt pans, while people who rely on public transport can take buses to either Marsalforn or Żebbuġ and then walk to the salt pans.  Even though it is possible to walk alongside the salt pans in some places, visitors should avoid stepping into the salt pans themselves, especially in the locations near Xwejni Bay with “no trespassing” signs.  Additionally, people should avoid littering, as the garbage could get blown into the salt pans and contaminate the salt.

coin-operated-grandmas-and-opium-den-dio.intro: A pier-side arcade of antique coin machines: Laughing Sal, fortune tellers and opium-den dioramas.
coin-operated-grandmas-and-opium-den-dio.html:
Located on Pier 45 in San Francisco, Musée Mecanique is one of the world's largest collections of antique coin-operated arcade machines; all restored in original working condition. Started by Edward Galland Zelinsky at the age of 11 in 1933 and expanded until his death in 2004, the museum is still maintained by his family to this day.

The museum offers free entry, but you might spend a quarter or two on one of its 300 machines as you navigate your way through its mazelike layout; why not measure the thrill of your kissing ability at the Kiss-O-Meter? Get your fortune read by an old soothsayer animatronic? Witness a diorama of a medieval execution? Or maybe just play some Space Invaders.

osaka-s-candy-colored-garbage-palace.intro: A working garbage incinerator dressed by Hundertwasser as a candy-coloured fantasy castle.
osaka-s-candy-colored-garbage-palace.html:
Imagine stumbling across a giant candy-colored palace on an artificial island in Osaka Bay, only to discover that it’s… a garbage incinerator!

That’s the Maishima Incineration Plant, designed by Austrian artist and architect Friedensreich Hundertwasser and opened in 2001.

While the outside looks like something out of a theme park, this plant actually processes waste, with tours taking visitors through viewing areas and educational exhibits explaining how Osaka deals with its rubbish. The guided tours are free and take about 90 minutes, although advance reservation is required.

tomb-of-christ-in-aomori.intro: Local legend says Jesus dodged the cross, fled to Aomori, farmed garlic and is buried on this hill.
tomb-of-christ-in-aomori.html:
According to the local legend, Jesus Christ was never crucified. Rather, his brother Isukiri took his place on the cross, and the real Jesus fled, for some reason carrying his brothers severed ear, across Siberia to northern Japan. He settled in a small rural Aomori village, became a garlic farmer, married a local woman named Miyuko, had three daughters, and quietly lived out his days until the age of 106. There are two mounds at Jesus's burial site. One for Jesus, the other for his brother's ear and his mother's hair.

The story traces back to 1935, when a man named Takeuchi Kiyomaro showed up with an ancient looking document (now widely regarded as fabricated) stating that these old burial mounds were the resting place of Christ. The villagers had no idea what to make of it, as there were no Christians in the area. The documents themselves were conveniently destroyed during the war, and the version that survives is a reconstruction published decades later by Kōsaka Wadō, a self-described cosmo-archaeologist whose other claim to fame was summoning a UFO on Japanese television. It sits in a glass case in the village museum, signed "Jesus Christ, Father of Christmas."

The village, to its credit, leaned all the way in. In 1964 it founded a tourist association and held the first Christ Festival, and every June since, a Shinto priest has performed a rite at the two mounds with the village mayor presiding over it as chief celebrant. Somewhere between 20,000 and 40,000 people a year now turn up to a village of 2,500 just to see this odd festival. In 2004, the Israeli ambassador even visited and donated an actual stone from the walls of Jerusalem.

The gift shop next to the grave is arguably the best part of the whole experience. They combine everything from pyramids, to UFO's, and all sorts of crazy conspiracies in one building. And to make things stranger, the entire place is owned and kept running by a local yogurt factory, whose drinking yogurt is naturally also for sale here.

a-soviet-prison-doubles-as-a-swimming-ho.intro: A flooded Soviet prison camp. Swim over the cell blocks and sunbathe on the spoil heap.
a-soviet-prison-doubles-as-a-swimming-ho.html:
Less than an hour's drive southwest of Tallinn, Estonia, a half-submerged cell block sticks out of turquoise water, bars still on some of the windows.

Rummu was a limestone quarry worked by prisoners from the late 1930s onward, absorbed into the Soviet forced-labor camp system after 1940. In 1991, Estonia regained its independence an not long afterward, the quarry was abandoned.

When the pumps that kept the pit dry finally shut off, groundwater did the rest fast. Buildings, machinery, whatever the guards didn't haul away, all of it went under.

These days, some visitors take the precarious path up the chalk-white quarry hill, looking down at the prison ruin from above. Others jump into the lake and swim right into the ruin itself, in through the windows and down the flooded halls. Divers explore what lies deeper beneath the surface.

A labor camp turned into an unlikely beach idyll, with the bars still in view.

700-year-old-church-devoured-by-sand.intro: A 1300s church the dunes swallowed. Only the tower still shows above the sand.
700-year-old-church-devoured-by-sand.html:
The Sand-Covered Church (Danish: Den TIlsandede kirke), officially named the St. Laurentii Church, is estimated to have been built in the 1300s, and was in its time the biggest in the area. Located on the very top of Denmark and one kilometer from the coastline, the sand started migrating towards the church by the 1600s. By the 1700s the battle against the sand meant that the congregation of the church had to dig out the entrance every time there was to be a church service.

The church was officially closed in 1795 by order of the king and the main building was torn down to be repurposed in 1810. Today only the church tower stands, open to any visitor who wants to ascend its narrow staircase to the top of the bell tower.

the-city-of-cable-cars-frozen-in-time.intro: A mining town strung with Soviet-era cable cars. Rusty cabins still cross the gorge.
the-city-of-cable-cars-frozen-in-time.html:
Chiatura is a city you cannot forget.

It lies deep in the gorge of the Kvirila River, in the heart of Georgia. Once, it was a thriving industrial center, with manganese mining, thousands of workers, and monumental Stalinist architecture. But above all, it was home to a network of 17 cable cars, one of which became the first passenger cable railway in the Soviet Union.

Today, Chiatura is a time machine. The old cabins, still carrying locals across the gorge, remember the 1950s. Riding them means stepping into another era. Some lines still operate, while others rust away at stations decorated with Soviet mosaics. Palaces of culture, abandoned mines, and empty houses: everything here feels suspended,waiting.

But there is another side to this place. Chiatura is fading. In 2016, the cable cars were declared unsafe, and in 2018, they were added to the Europa Nostra list of Europe's most endangered heritage sites. Some lines have been modernized, but they no longer carry the raw, gritty character that made the city so special.

Now is the last window of opportunity to see Chiatura as it really is, without tourist crowds or glass gondolas with air conditioning. Just you, the cables above the gorge, the creak of old metal, and the silence that still echoes with the breath of a lost era.

This place is not just a dot on a map. It is a conversation with history, one you can still have while it's still alive.

berlin-s-hill-of-nazi-rubble-cold-war-sp.intro: A hill of Nazi rubble topped by a Cold War listening station, now a sprawling graffiti canvas.
berlin-s-hill-of-nazi-rubble-cold-war-sp.html:
Teufelsberg, literally "Devil's Mountain," rises 394 feet (120 m) out of the Grunewald forest on the western edge of Berlin. The hill is built from roughly 26 million tons of WWII rubble, dumped there between 1950 and 1972 over an unfinished Nazi military-technical college designed by Albert Speer. Engineers tried blowing the building up first; when that failed, they buried it instead.

In 1963 the US National Security Agency built one of its largest Cold War listening stations on top, part of the global ECHELON network, and ran it around the clock until the Berlin Wall came down. The distinctive white radomes, dome-shaped covers for the antennas underneath, are still there, giving the hill its distinctive skyline.

After the Americans left, the site fell into disrepair and became a popular spot for urban explorers. It eventually opened for legal, ticketed visits. Today, murals cover walls, stairwells, and towers across the site. Teufelsberg is now one of Europe's largest street art galleries, with great views over Berlin.

a-melodic-sculpture-in-the-lancashire-co.intro: A galvanised-steel sculpture on the moors that sings when the wind moves through its pipes.
a-melodic-sculpture-in-the-lancashire-co.html:
The Singing Ringing Tree is a modern sculpture (which has no connection to the 1957 film of the same name) that was constructed in 2006 as part of an initiative by Mid Pennine Arts to beautify Lancashire’s countryside. The sculpture, which was designed by Mike Tonkin and Anna Liu, consists of a series of pipes stacked on top of each other to form a 3-meter-tall structure with a columnar center and a fan-like top. What makes this sculpture notable is that the individual pipes produce tones as the wind blows through them, resulting in an ethereal-sounding melody, and this melody will change depending on which way the wind blows and how strong the wind is.

The quirky sculpture has not only garnered the love of the nearby cities’ residents but has also earned several awards, including the National Award of the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) for architectural excellence in 2007. Additionally, in 2015, it was named by a panel of experts sponsored by The Independent Newspaper and British Airways travel magazine as one of 21 landmarks that define Britain in the twenty-first century.

Despite its fame, the Singing Ringing Tree receives relatively few visitors, mainly because of its remote location in the countryside to the south of Burnley, England. Reaching the location by car is relatively easy; people can just drive south from Burnley on Crown Point Road to a parking area just west of the sculpture and then walk 10 minutes down a dirt trail to reach the sculpture. However, no public transportation travels to the area, so people without cars would either need to walk for over an hour from the center of Burnley or about 50 minutes from Towneley Park on the southern outskirts of Burnley to reach the site. Nonetheless, the sculpture and its music will reward anyone willing to put in the effort to make the trip.

Contributed by Wayfarer

frozen-aquarium-in-miyagi.html:
Instead of fish tanks, each fish here is frozen, unmoving, in a large block of ice. An ice company that supplies the local fishing port with industrial ice spent years developing a proprietary technique to produce what it calls jun-koori, or pure ice that's free of impurities. The ice is so transparent that the frozen fish look like they're simply behind glass.

Each block takes a full week to freeze, since they have to drop the temperature slowly and precisely to prevent the cloudiness caused by rapid freezing. The result is ice so perfectly clear you can see straight through. It was also a shock to see what kinds of fish they had displayed here. They had rays, multiple octopi, and even a few sharks! But the coolest part here is how they present the fish.

The room is a fully rigged with projection lights. Each crystal clear "aquarium" alternating colors from tropical blues, deep reds, lime greens. And occasionally they have this unnecessarily cinematic projection show that serves no purpose other than to wow visitors, and I was certainly wowed.

The aquarium opened inside the city's market complex in 2002. The room is maintained at minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit) year-round. Visitors are issued free thermal overcoats that make you feel like as if you are in one of those Hollywood environmental doomsday films where the world turns to ice. As you step through the door, the temperature change is immediately felt. The initial shock was certainly cold but once it gets to 10 minutes in there you really feel your fingers start to freeze.

The original attraction drew more than 100,000 visitors per year and inspired imitation pop-up ice aquariums. Then the earthquake and tsunami of March 11, 2011 struck, and the market building was hit and ruined.

The ice company survived and spent the following six years rebuilding, eventually opening again in 2017. The current installation is larger and more refined than the original, with additional ice sculptures of the city's mascot character Hoya-boya found alongside the frozen specimens and a mural by a Belgian street artist covering the entrance wall. Alongside the aquarium, the ice company runs factory tours, sells flower-ice gifts (seasonal flowers frozen into presentation blocks), caters outdoor events with live ice sculpting, and even operates a kitchen stall in the market. Note: Admission is cash only.

south-london-s-most-notable-street-art-l.html:
In 2008, the street artist Bansky organized an event called the Cans Festival in Lambeth within South London. Various street artists were invited to repaint the Leake Street tunnel, a neglected Victorian-era tunnel running underneath the train tracks departing from Waterloo Station. After the festival, the tunnel was completely covered in graffiti.

This event changed Leake Street forever. People would continue to paint new street art over the old street art (inevitably painting over Bansky’s works as well, which would be unthinkable today), and the site became a trendy place to go. The street was eventually pedestrianized, and restaurants, bars, and clubs moved into the various spaces adjoining the tunnel.

Leake Street today is recognized as one of London’s most notable legal walls (a place where graffiti can be sprayed without worries about being arrested). Tourists looking for alternative places to visit will walk through the tunnels, and new generations of street artists can routinely be found at work producing new creations. The tunnel even has its own website with information about the tunnel’s businesses, rules for painting in and using the tunnel, and contact details for organizing events and obtaining permits for commercial photography and filming. Note that photographing the tunnels for non-commercial purposes is highly encouraged.

The entrances to the tunnel are located just south of Waterloo Station. The west entrance (which is wheelchair-accessible) is just off of York Road, while the east entrance (which has stairs) can be reached from the pedestrianized street named Lower Marsh. The tunnel is always open and always reasonably well lit (although a tripod might be needed for photography), and it is also as safe as any other part of Central London to walk around. The street art is always changing, so people who live in or frequently visit London may want to return about once every year or so.

Contributed by Wayfarer

the-small-fake-castle-on-top-of-a-hill-i.html:
Mow Cop Castle, which consists of a stone turret attached to an extended section of wall by a pointed arch, was originally built in 1754 by Randle Wilbraham, a notable local landowner, lawyer, and minister of parliament.  The small folly stands very prominently on a hill named Mow Cop where it could easily be seen from Wilbraham’s residence at Rode Hall.  Although the folly looks completely non-functional today, the turret originally had a pointed roof and functioned as a small summer home for Wilbraham’s family.

The castle today is owned by the National Trust, which has taken efforts to preserve the folly and also to secure the interior of the turret.  A small village with historic links to Methodism has grown around the hill over the centuries, and the castle has become the defining symbol of the local community.

Mow Cop Castle is free to visit and can be accessed 24 hours a day.  The castle is easily accessed via a network of short trails surrounding the hill; walking from the surrounding streets up to the folly should take between 5 and 10 minutes.  Note that the paths are unsuitable for wheelchairs.  People driving to the site can use the car park on the west side of the hill.  People using public transport can take a bus from Kidsgrove to Mow Cop, although the bus does not run on Sundays.

User-Generated Content

Usage Data

We automatically collect information about how you interact with DeepSpot, including pages visited, features used, spots saved, and search queries. This helps us improve the platform and understand what our community values.

fermented-shark-in-greenland.html:
Too easily, travelers outside their own countries are reluctant to try foods that they consider unappealing or strange. Often, this hesitation can simply be chalked up to what a person has or hasn't been exposed to regularly in their own culture. For instance, some people may find the thought of eating a heavy, greasy American hamburger with American "cheese" to be offputting, while others may turn their noses up at balut, a dish made with a fertilized bird egg that's eaten in multiple Asian countries including the Philippines, Thailand, and Cambodia. Further north, we have Greenland, a country that has its own food that tends to make visitors pause, and that dish is known as hákarl.

Hákarl is a historical food that is made from fermented Greenland shark, a gray sleeper shark that can live up to half a millenium (yes, that's a full 500 years). These ancient beasts often weigh over 2,000 pounds, providing plenty of meat for all types of creative recipes. And this is where hákarl comes in.

Before we jump in, we've got to be honest. We did leave out a crucial reason the uninitiated tend to snub this dish. Frankly, it smells like urine. If you find yourself sitting at the dinner table with a plate of hákarl before you, your first question is going to undoubtedly be, "Why the heck does my food smell like pee?" That's because sharks' digestive systems are kidney-less, and their bodies hold urine in their skin. The urine-related organic compounds, urea and trimethylamine oxide, in the shark's body give the dish its characteristic smell. As you might imagine, eating the shark's flesh in its natural state can give people some serious health issues. In fact, it's poisonous and can cause blindness or even death.

So how did Greenlanders end up creating a perfectly safe dish from this toxic ingredient? Now, most people might think a shark that smells like urine is best left alone in nature and not exactly fair game for eating. But the industrious Greenlanders decided hundred of years ago that a fun little experiment would be to gut and bury one of the sharks in a pit for a few months and see if that made it taste better. And they didn't stop there. Once they dug it up, they decided to let it dry for another five months or so, just for good measure. To everyone's surprise, the shark did in fact taste much better (and didn't kill anyone), and thus, hákarl was born. In the cold environment, the dish became a staple food that helped locals survive harsh winters.

Today, the fermentation methods have changed a bit, with the sharks initially kept in storage boxes before being dried outside. Even after this long process, the shark does still have a strong ammonia smell, but many people say that after giving the dish a few tries, the taste does in fact grow on you. If all else fails, you can always drink the bit of schnapps that is traditionally served with the hákarl and give a healthy dose of respect to the people who not only figured out a way to make a poisonous shark edible, but who also have the stomachs to eat it.

the-man-from-the-basement-the-siberian-s.html:
In the quiet Siberian city of Berdsk, where life flows slowly and calmly, something completely alien rises. A huge red‑brick building with pointed towers, which was supposed to become a school, but instead became a ghost. For over a decade, it has stood in eternal neglect, construction halted abruptly, leaving behind only concrete skeletons of staircases and walls that never heard children's voices.

Inside, there is absolute silence, broken only by the echo of your own footsteps. Endless corridors with bare brick walls stretch into the darkness, and dead metal ventilation ducts and tangled wires hang frozen under the ceiling. Huge windows with arched frames let in the only light, casting shadows on piles of abandoned tiles, construction debris, and forgotten tools. It seems as if the workers simply vanished mid‑task.

But the most terrifying thing here is not in the dark rooms, but in the heart of the building: an open elevator shaft. It pierces all four floors, yawning like a black void with no barriers. One wrong step, and you disappear into that abyss forever. Such traps do not forgive mistakes. There is no second chance. The city tried to sell this unfinished building for hundreds of millions of rubles, but no buyers ever came, leaving it alone with its silence.

A narrow, crumbling staircase leads down into a vast basement. This place is truly a labyrinth of horror: dozens of small and enormous rooms alternate, and the corridors twist so much that you lose all sense of direction. There, the darkness is absolute and impenetrable. The windows are overgrown with thick grass, and the only light is the beam of a flashlight, revealing red wires snaking across the concrete floor like the veins of this dead building. It feels as if this labyrinth stretches endlessly, swallowing anyone who dares to descend too deep.

Many adventurers have tried to get inside, but this place does not forgive carelessness. Crumbling ceilings, the absence of light, and deadly open shafts make this building one of the most dangerous locations in the region.

It is said that a teenager once disappeared here. They searched for him but never found him. Since then, locals avoid the basements, and children tell each other stories about the "Man from the Basement." Some claim that at night, a strange sound comes from the elevator shaft, as if someone is calling for help.

If you climb to the very top, under the wooden roof arches, you see the ordinary world: white apartment buildings, greenery, and the calm of a provincial town. This contrast is more frightening than any darkness. Outside — the world of the living. But here, within these walls, a foreign, unrealized dream is frozen, once valued at hundreds of millions of rubles, but ultimately left unwanted by anyone.

This is not just an abandoned building. It is a concrete monument to an unfinished dream, which no one ever decided to complete.

the-ghost-of-moscow-the-hospital-that-st.html:
In the 1990s, rumors circulated in Moscow about a place that wasn't marked on any map. People said that the hopes of a generation had died there, and that footsteps could be heard in the corridors at night. This place was called Khovrinka, and it became the darkest myth of the capital.

In the early 1980s, it was supposed to be the most modern hospital in Moscow, with 1,300 beds, unique architecture, and state-of-the-art equipment. By 1985, the building was almost complete. Furniture and equipment had been delivered. All that remained was to open the doors. But they never opened.

Construction was frozen. First temporarily, then forever.

The reason turned out to be simpler and more terrifying than any legend: the hospital had been built on a swampy wasteland, directly above the Likhoborka River, which had been enclosed in a pipe. The ground was unstable, the building began to sink, and the basements flooded. Enormous sums of money were needed to fix the problems, but the crumbling country no longer had the means.

So a dream turned into a concrete sarcophagus.

And then the worst began.

Without security, without walls, without light, Khovrinka became a refuge for outcasts, drug addicts, and those who wanted to disappear from sight. But the building itself was a death trap: open elevator shafts, collapsing ceilings, and exposed rebar jutting from the walls. People fell, got lost, and died.

Someone wrote on the wall:

"This hospital is a land of wonders. Step inside and you'll disappear."

These words became the epitaph for all its dark fame.

And then the legends were born.

It was said that a Satanic cult operated in the basements, conducting black masses and making human sacrifices. According to the story, special forces raided the site, drove the cultists into an underground tunnel, and collapsed it, burying them alive. There is no evidence for this, but the story was passed from mouth to mouth like a frightening fairy tale.

Others noticed a resemblance between the building and the logo from the movie Resident Evil and believed that it was not a hospital at all, but a secret laboratory. And in the flooded basements, it was rumored that there was a freezing pool that never dried up, above which thick fog hung even in summer.

But the most chilling part was that these legends blended with reality.

In 2005, the body of a young man was found in one of the elevator shafts. It was said that he had committed suicide because of unrequited love. A small memorial appeared at the site of his death, where people still leave flowers and cigarettes. Bodies were regularly found on the grounds of Khovrinka: homeless people, victims of crime, and those who had simply fallen into the void.

People were afraid of it, but it pulled them in.

In 2018, the hospital was demolished. A residential complex was built on its site. Physically, Khovrinka no longer exists.

But it hasn't disappeared.

It lives on in myths, in photographs, and in the stories of those who managed to see it. It has moved from concrete into memory and has become one of Moscow's darkest urban legends. One of the city's most chilling pages, which can now only be found in stories.

victoria-boundary-stones-the-former-mark.html:
If you’ve ever strolled through the bustling city of Hong Kong and noticed some unusual small granite obelisks, you might have wondered what they were. These seemingly out-of-place structures are called boundary stones, used as markers for Victoria City, and today are the remnants of Hong Kong's bygone British colonial era.

In the 1800s, the British government expanded Victoria due to the rapidly growing economy of this busy harbour city. In 1903, several stones were erected as physical markers for the area. These spanned from the edge of the city, with placements in Kennedy Town, Mount Davis, Sandy Bay Gap, Lung Fu Shan, the Mid-Levels, and Happy Valley. Seeing all 10 stones would mean a six-hour trek covering over 21.5km, with approximately 300 metres of elevation gain.

​

Boundary Stone 1 - Sai Ning Road, Kennedy Town

To start the trek, we start with the one boundary stone that has been re-erected to a different but close location. It was originally placed in what is now Serene Court; however, due to land developments in the 1970s, the obelisk was moved to Kennedy Town’s Recreation Ground on Sai Ning Street.

Boundary Stone 2 - Mount Davis

As we head further south, we will reach Mount Davis. Today, the area is affluent due to the influx of luxury homes. However, back in British colonial times, Mount Davis was an artillery depot of the British Armed Forces. There was a common misconception that only 7 boundary stones were erected; however, in late 2021, the 3 missing stones were located. Fortunately, off-the-beaten-path hiking enthusiasts located the stone, and Hong Kong’s Antiquities and Monuments Office authenticated it.

Boundary Stone 3 - Pok Fu Lam Road, Sandy Bay Gap

Pok Fu Lam village was home to several of Hong Kong’s firsts. The iconic floral emblem (Hong Kong Orchid Tree) was found in the area, its first reservoir and its first dairy farm. As you head down Mount Davis, towards Sandy Bay Gap, you will come across this boundary stone in the midst of Pok Fu Lam Road.

Boundary Stone 4, 5 - Hatton Road, Lung Fu Shan

As we make our way inwards to the centre of Victoria, we enter Lung Fu Shan. Formerly known as Dragon Tiger Mountain, the area was home to British military defences due to its strategic high elevation overlooking the western area. The fourth boundary stone was lost and forgotten due to thick jungle vegetation, but was uncovered in late 2021. The fifth stone is on Hatton Road.

​

Boundary Stone 6, 7, 8, 9 - Mid Levels

As we traverse east, we arrive at the Mid Levels, the home of Hong Kong’s affluent. In the 19th Century, the area became well known for its larger mansions with garden terraces that overlooked Victoria Harbour. During the 1860s, Franklin D. Roosevelt’s mother, Sara, resided here during the American Civil War.

Before late 2021, Boundary Stone 9 was not found until local hiking and history enthusiasts stumbled across this obelisk on a slope near Rosaryhill School.

​

Boundary Stone 10 - Wong Nai Chung Road, Happy Valley

Our last and final boundary stone of Victoria resides in Happy Valley, formerly known as Wong Nai Chung Valley. The area was prominent for its abundance of rice paddies, receiving nourishment from the yellow mud stream from the Wong Nai Chung Gap. In the 1800s, the British military established a camp in the area, but rising cases of malaria soon forced them to retreat. With the death rate increasing, the area became a burial ground. It would ironically be called Happy Valley. In 1846, the British Government proposed and developed the land from rice paddies into today’s Happy Valley Racecourse.

colombian-national-symbol-hats.html:
There's something beautiful about places that have perfected the art of doing or making something. For instance, in Central America, there's Tequila, Mexico, home of its namesake alcohol. Across the pond, a Venitian island, Murano, is famous for its 1000-year-old glassblowing tradition. In Roquefort, France, the villagers make a special blue cheese from sheep's milk, and their process has been perfected to such that no other place in the world can officially claim to make "Roquefort cheese."

Travel to South American and make a stop in Tuchín, a town in Córdoba, Colombia. You won't have to spend much time wondering what their particular specialty is. That's because you'll notice it right away: the sombrero vueltiao, a colorful hat that is perhaps the most notable symbol of not just the town, but the entire country. In English, the term "sombrero vueltiao" means "turned hat," and it refers to the method of braiding and working fiber strands use to design the hat.

In Tuchín, most of the 50,000 or so residents identify as Zenú, an indigenous group that has called the area home for thousands of years. Today, nearly all of the town's Zenú residents participate in the intricate hat-making process that has evolved over time. These hats have become so internationally famous that both Bill Clinton and Pope John Paul II have worn them at some point. Sombreros vueltiaos originally served a less prestigious purpose than adorning the heads of famous political and religious leaders. The hats were first intended simply to protect peasants from the sun as they worked. Throughout the centuries, the hats gained status and are now a symbol of pride and the Colombian town's incredible artistry.

A sombrero vueltiao is recognizable by its detailed designs that are often black and white but also come in a combination of bright colors like red, yellow, and blue. It can take multiple weeks to make just one hat, and once you've learned a little about the process, you'll quickly understand why. They're constructed from parts of the local caña flecha plant, a type of green cane plant with a thick stalk and which is found in abundance near Colombian rivers. Craftsman as young as five or six begin working with the cane fibers, learning to select the perfect plants before boiling the fibers, allowing them to dry thoroughly in the sun, and then dyeing them vibrant colors.

The completed black and white hats almost have a Tim Burton vibe to them with their high contrast color scheme, but rather than telling odd, Burton-esque stories, sombreros vueltiaos tell stories of Colombian life and culture. No matter the color of the hat, it's always decorated with symbols (called "pintas") that can represent the artist themselves, nature, or community stories. Some sombreros vueltiaos use 27 cane fibers in each braided strand, making them the most complex and revered of the hats. Ones that use fewer fibers take considerably less time to create and are much less expensive.

While men have historically crafted and worn the sombrero vueltiao, they've now become popular with women as well. In Tuchín, you'll see just about every local wearing one at some point, whether it's at a festival or other important event or simply around town. Visitors can take watch the traditional hat-making process and even attend workshops to try their hand at the special South American skill.

If you're lucky enough to visit the town, don't overlook this cultural symbol that is part fashion statement, part practical UV-protection, and 100% true artisanship.

japanese-women-divers.html:
If you ever played mermaids (or mermen) as a child, you probably realized you couldn't cut it being an actual mythical creature, considering you could only hold your breath for a few seconds. But there's a special group of women in Japan who are as close to the legendary sea creatures as you can get. But their time in the water isn't spent playing or sunbathing on rocks. On the contrary, these "mermaids" work incredibly hard and demonstrate impressive athletic ability that continues to awe people from around the world.

Known as ama divers, these women make their living on the Shima Peninsula in Mie Prefecture. While one might initially be tempted to summarize their work as simply "pearl diving," the fact is, their skills go way beyond just finding gorgeous gemstones hidden away in oyster shells. These women form an elite group that is specially trained to safely navigate the ocean depths, swimming through currents and keeping an astounding work pace. The ama diving tradition is thousands of years old, and modern women have studied the knowledge passed down through the millenia to achieve these nearly miraculous feats.

While men were sometimes ama divers in the past, today, the practice is solely performed by women and is often passed from mother to daughter. For thousands of years, these women have been diving for sea urchines, abalone, and sea snails and using basic tools to extract their bounty from the ocean's depths. The term "ama" itself means "sea woman," and these divers are so reliant on the ocean that many pray to the sea gods for protection before starting their work each morning.

Some ama divers perform their work all on their own and can make as many as 60 dives in just one hour. To keep up this pace, they have developed a very specific method of breathing before and after each dive, ensuring they always have enough oxygen and adjust to pressure changes safely. Their training enables them to hold their breath for up to two minutes at a time, which is amazing, considering the physical effort their work takes. Other divers work with a partner (many times, this is the woman's husband), a method that allows the diver to reach further depths on each dive. None use special equipment and instead rely on their fine-tuned work processes to carry out their work. In fact, the women used to dive without any clothing minus a headscarf. Even today, they only wear wetsuits with the scarves, and still, a few wear only a thin, traditional cotton outfit that doesn't offer much warmth.

As you might guess, this extreme type of work doesn't appeal to much of the contemporary working population. That's why there are only an estimated 2,000 or so ama divers left, a steep decline from the 10,000 or so that existed around 1950. Hopefully, the tradition continues, as ama divers have gained near-mythic status themselves. The next time you're out on a boat in Japan, keep your eyes peeled. You might just spot a real-life mermaid, or, even better, a real-life ama diver!

melon-heads-urban-legend.html:
If you've ever sat around a campfire and listened to someone tell scary stories, you've probably heard the familiar ones. Tales of Bigfoot, UFO abductions, and ghostly hitchhikers are a dime a dozen. But have you heard the one about the melon-headed children running around certain areas of the United States? These supernatural entities are as bizarre as they are alarming to all who have witnessed them.

The kids are said to have freakishly large heads and miniature bodies that make them unmistakable should you encounter one running past you in the woods. Officially known as "Melon Heads" by locals, these child-creatures are both beloved and feared among the community. Many stories about these oddly shaped kids originate from Ohio, but the spooky beings have also been known to roam around Michigan and Connecticut.

Like most urban legends, the details can be murky and tend to change depending on the location. The basic story is that these kids were once imprisoned in an asylum where they were experimented on by a mad, deranged scientist. The experiments led to the children growing overly large, hairless heads. Legend says the children banded together to escape from their tormentor (sometimes called Dr. Crow), and they now roam the woods, never growing up due to their mutant DNA.

Ohio has one version of the melon head story that pinpoints the location of Dr. Crow's institution to its own state, specifically in Chardon Township in Geauga County. This variation states that the United States government hired a certain Dr. Crow to treat children with a medical condition called hydrocephalus, which causes a person's head to fill with fluid and swell. The Dr. Crow in this version owned an orphanage and experimented on the children, causing their bodies to mutate. Their heads grew even larger and the rest of their bodies shrank. At some point, the kids banded together to overthrow and kill the demented doctor, burning down the orphanage and forever hating all humans. The melon heads then formed their own population in the woods, occasionally leaving to kidnap and/or eat non-melon heads. Today, an abandoned, crumbling house remains in the woods of Geauga County and locals say you can catch a glimpse of a melon head around the ruins every now and then. Conversely, Michigan also claims to be the original home of the melon heads, citing the Felt Mansion in Saugatuck as the most likely place to see one of the mythical creatures.

The less exciting version of the story is that Dr. Crow was genuinely trying to help the children and when he died of natural causes, the children decided to stick around the orphanage and keep to themselves. Rather than eating humans, these melon heads are just misunderstood and shy. A third story mentions Dr. Crow killing his own wife, much to the ire of the children who sought revenge and burned down the home.

Still, some people say melon heads don't have anything to do with a doctor. Instead, it's said the children are from an inbred family that hid in the woods from the outside community. Some Reddit users suggest this version of the story is based on a real family, but there's no evidence this is true. All of the melon head stories, both the Dr. Crow and inbred family ones, suggest that the children formed their own secret population and stick together to this day.

Suffice it to say, this is one campfire story that will grab your friends' attention -- and have them looking over their shoulder when the sun goes down. If you're in your tent and see a melon-headed silhouette, it's best to keep the tent closed and hope they're the introverted Melon Heads, not the cannibal Melon Heads . . .

disappearing-lake-in-austria.html:
Some places you love to visit more than once over the years, in the hopes of reliving the wonderful memories from that very first visit. However, Gruner See, a special lake in Austria, will almost certainly give you a different experience each time you go. Known in English as "Green Lake," this body of water does something other lakes don't: it disappears and returns each year, taking the local park with it.

Gruner See is virtually nonexistent from fall to early spring, but you can enjoy taking in the mountain scenery from the benches that fill the park. At this time, the lake is more of a tiny pond, if that. However, the prime time to come is in late spring or early summer when the lake grows drastically in size. Formed by runoff from snow and ice on the nearby Hochschwab Mountains, the lake is incredibly clear with a glass-like appearance. The bright grass underneath makes the water look a startlingly vibrant shade of emerald green straight from the Land of Oz. Gruner See draws visitors from around the world, eager to snap photos of the idyllic setting. Fish and crabs fill the lake, not bothered by the seasonal changes.

Starting in the fall, the lake begins to disappear again, revealing the park once more. Snow begins to cover the area, including the mountains, all in preparation for next year's ice melt. During this time, several bridges and trees that were submerged become visible agian, and the area takes on another type of charm. The winter wonderland is just as lovely, only in a different way.

forum.title: Underrated Region of Japan: Tohoku
forum.body:
As someone who lives and works within the Japanese travel industry, I find it genuinely surprising how frequently the Tohoku region is bypassed by international visitors. In many ways, it feels even more overlooked than Shikoku, the smallest and least-populated of the four main islands. While the crowds flock to the well-trodden paths of the Golden Route, they are missing the soul of the north.
My top recommendation for anyone planning a trip to Japan, particularly during the humid summer months, is to look toward Tohoku. While the rest of the country swelters, you will find yourself enveloped by the refreshing, cool mountain breezes that sweep across the northern landscapes. Imagine wandering through high-altitude, vibrant flower fields atop the northern plateaus, where the air is crisp and the scenery feels untouched by time.
Beyond the natural splendor, Tohoku is home to charming, sometimes hauntingly eerie locations that possess a profound sense of history. As these rural areas become increasingly endangered by depopulation, they offer a rare, unfiltered glimpse into a vanishing way of life. There is a quiet, melancholic beauty here that is impossible to find in the bustling city centers. Once you experience the depth of Tohoku’s atmosphere and the warmth of its people, you will likely find yourself hooked, compelled to return year after year to uncover even more of its well-kept secrets.
